facts.text: Castro Pretorio derives its name from the ancient Castra Praetoria, the Praetorian Guard barracks built by Tiberius in 23 AD and later incorporated into the Aurelian Walls.
The neighborhood’s most famous square, Piazza della Repubblica, was once called Piazza Esedra and sits where Via Nazionale meets Via Cavour, linking the train station to Rome’s historic center.
In 1870, Italian troops breached Porta Pia, a gate in the area, ending the Papal States and opening Rome to the Kingdom of Italy.
The Castra Praetoria’s site still hosts an Italian Army garrison today, making it the world’s oldest continuously used military barracks.
The Baths of Diocletian, built between 298 and 306 AD to serve nearby hills, leave ruins visible along Via Cernaia and in Piazza dei Cinquecento within Castro Pretorio.
The area once housed the infamous Campus Sceleratus, where Vestal virgins who broke their vows were buried alive, located just outside Porta Collina.
